title: Higher or lower?
hook: A number from 1 to 1,000. You only hear "higher" or "lower". How few guesses do you need?

doesNotKnow: powers of two beyond small ones

misconception: Searching a bigger range takes proportionally more guesses: 1,000 numbers needs something like 50 or 100 guesses, and twice the range needs twice the guesses.
objective: The learner can explain that guessing the middle throws away half of what is left each time, so 1,000 numbers need at most 10 guesses and doubling the range adds only one guess.

claims.text: Always guessing the middle of what is still possible finds any number from 1 to 1,000 in at most 10 guesses.
claims.source: Binary search on n sorted items needs at most floor(log2 n) + 1 comparisons; n = 1000 gives floor(9.97) + 1 = 10. Knuth, TAOCP Vol. 3, 6.2.1 (Algorithm B and its analysis).

claims.text: In the worst case the numbers still possible after each wrong middle guess go 500, 250, 125, 62, 31, 15, 7, 3, 1.
claims.source: Guessing the middle of m candidates and being wrong leaves at most floor(m/2): 1000 -> 500 -> 250 -> 125 -> 62 -> 31 -> 15 -> 7 -> 3 -> 1; nine wrong guesses, so the tenth is right.

claims.text: A million numbers need at most 20 middle guesses, and a billion need at most 30.
claims.source: floor(log2 10^6) + 1 = floor(19.93) + 1 = 20; floor(log2 10^9) + 1 = floor(29.90) + 1 = 30. Knuth, TAOCP Vol. 3, 6.2.1.

claims.text: Doubling the range adds exactly one guess to the worst case.
claims.source: floor(log2 2n) + 1 = (floor(log2 n) + 1) + 1, since log2 2n = log2 n + 1.

claims.text: A guess in the middle of what is still possible rules out at least half of it, whichever way the answer goes; the stage calls a guess that keeps more than half a weak guess.
claims.source: With m candidates and the middle one guessed, a wrong answer leaves at most floor(m/2): the lesson's mid = floor((lo+hi)/2) leaves lo..mid-1 or mid+1..hi, sizes mid-lo and hi-mid, both <= floor(m/2) (checked for every m up to 2000 in artifacts/scratch/fc2-binary-search.mjs). Seen in the reveal ("rules out half of it, whichever way the answer goes"). The guess itself counts as ruled out. Added by fact-checker 2026-10-12; needs an independent check.

claims.text: A sorted list of 2,000 names needs at most 11 middle checks to find one name.
claims.source: floor(log2 2000) + 1 = floor(10.97) + 1 = 11; exhaustive run of the lesson's middle rule over all 2,000 positions gives max 11. Recall question and its why ("1,000 needs 10; doubling to 2,000 adds just one"). Assumes one three-way check (less / equal / greater) per step, as in the guessing game. Added by fact-checker 2026-10-12; needs an independent check.

claims.text: After a wrong middle guess, what is left is the worst-case count or one fewer: with 1 to 1,000, "lower than 500" leaves 499 while "higher than 500" leaves 500.
claims.source: With m candidates and mid = floor((lo+hi)/2), the two sides have mid-lo and hi-mid numbers: equal when m is odd, floor(m/2)-1 and floor(m/2) when m is even. For 1..1000, mid = 500: 1..499 (499) or 501..1000 (500). Reveal paragraph 1 (v2), added after learner finding 4 (499 on screen vs 500 in text).

recall.question: A sorted list holds 2,000 names. Checking the middle each time, what is the most checks you could need to find one name?
recall.why: Each check halves what is left. 1,000 needs 10; doubling to 2,000 adds just one.
